sections.h2: Seller costs set by Wisconsin law
sections.html:
Three duties fall on a Wisconsin seller by statute: paying the transfer fee on the deed, covering recording for any paper the seller has to file, and giving the buyer a condition report. Commission, title charges and how the year's property tax is split work differently, because your contract and settlement statement control them.

Start by pricing the transfer fee. It is created by Wis. Stat. 77.22, falls on the grantor, and is paid at the register of deeds' counter when the deed is recorded. Recording the document is a separate flat $30. The rest is negotiable, so have the closing agent write out an estimate before you sign.

The rate works out to 30 cents on every $100 of value. Any piece of $100 left over counts as a whole $100.

"Value" is a defined term. Under Wis. Stat. 77.21(3), a conveyance that isn't a gift is valued at everything actually paid or promised, liens on the property included. Gifts, deeds for token consideration and exchanges are valued at an estimated open-market price. Land contracts use the principal the buyer promises to pay.

sections.h2: Seller charges and deadlines at a glance
sections.html:
Charge or dutyAmount or deadlineStatute
Transfer feeThirty cents on each $100 of value, rounded up; the grantor owes itWis. Stat. 77.22(1)
Recording the deedFlat $30 for each documentWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag)
Copy of a recorded document$2 for the first page, then $1 a page; certification costs $1 moreWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(b)
Condition report to buyerDue 10 days from contract acceptanceWis. Stat. 709.02(1)
Payoff statement from your lenderSeven business days from a written request on residential propertyWis. Stat. 708.15(3)

Recording fees are payable in advance by whoever asks the register for the service.

Only conveyances that match a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25 escape the fee, and the deed itself must name the exemption. Homeowners most often run into these:

  • An inheritance, whether by will, descent or survivorship.
  • Lender-side foreclosure outcomes, including a deed in lieu to a mortgage holder or a land contract seller.
  • A tax or assessment sale.
  • A trustee handing title to a beneficiary without real consideration.
  • A deed that fixes or confirms an earlier recorded conveyance and carries little or no consideration.
  • A deed whose only job is to give or release security for a debt unrelated to a conveyance.
  • A taking by condemnation, or land worth $1,000 or less.

When a land contract was recorded with the proper fee already paid, the seller's later deed is exempt too. Under 77.256, no city, village, town or county may add its own fee to an exempt conveyance.

A transfer return goes to the Department of Revenue with the value, the fee and any exemption, signed by both grantor and grantee. The register of deeds holds the conveyance until the completed return and fee arrive. Wis. Stat. 77.255 carves out a narrow set of cases that need no return.

Filing happens online in My Tax Account, with no username or password, and a filer can also view or amend a return there. In a normal sale, your title company or attorney handles the filing. If you sign a deed on your own, the RETR page offers guides and the exemption list.

Collected fees are shared under Wis. Stat. 77.24, with 20 percent staying in the county and the balance going to the state. The department can revisit a return later, billing more fee or refunding an overpayment when the value was misreported or an exemption was claimed in error.

For one-to-four unit properties, the seller must deliver a filled-in condition report within 10 days after accepting an offer. The form, set out in Wis. Stat. 709.03, asks about structure, mechanical systems, environmental issues, wells, septic and storage tanks, taxes and special assessments, permits, and land use.

A late report lets the buyer walk away for two business days once the 10 days expire, with the deposit returned. A seller who learned something before acceptance that alters an answer must send an amended report or an amendment inside the same 10 days. Treat the form as a disclosure, not a warranty, and it won't stand in for inspections.

A few sellers are excused: a court-appointed fiduciary, such as a personal representative, who never occupied the property; an owner of a property that has never been inhabited; and any transfer exempt from the fee. The chapter covers sales, exchanges and land contracts.

Send the lender a written payoff request. On a residential loan, the lender has 7 business days to answer. Under Wis. Stat. 708.15, the answer lists the payoff figure and what is needed to compute it for your chosen date, such as daily interest, along with a payment cutoff time and instructions for sending the money.

Pick a payoff date as far as 30 days out. Your authorized agent, such as the closing agent, can make the request for you. Residential lenders may not hedge the amount or say it could change before that date, which gives closing a firm number. Ask early.

Plan backward from closing day. Acceptance starts the condition report clock, so fill in the form before you list. Request the payoff statement and choose a payoff date that matches closing. Several days ahead, get the draft settlement statement from the title company or attorney and test the transfer fee against the value on the return.

On the day, both parties sign the transfer return and the deed changes hands. The fee and recording charge reach the register of deeds, your lender is paid from the sale money, and whatever remains is sent to you. A cash buyer can make the schedule quicker because no buyer's lender is underwriting, though your payoff, the fee and the report follow the same rules.

sections.h2: Questions to ask the closing agent
sections.html:
Get the estimate itemized, and match each line to the amounts above. These questions catch most surprises:

  • What value is being reported on the transfer return, and does it include any lien being paid off?
  • Is any exemption being claimed, and under which subsection of Wis. Stat. 77.25?
  • What is the per diem on my mortgage, and through what payoff date is the statement good?
  • What is the balance on the property tax bill, and how is the current year prorated?
  • Which charges come from the contract, such as commission, title and repair credits, and which come from statute?
  • Has the condition report been delivered, and on what date?

To learn the tax balance, call the treasurer, county or municipal, that bills the parcel; the printed bill shows which office collects. If you sell for cash as-is, many of these lines shrink, though the transfer fee, recording and your payoff still apply.

faqs.q: Which side pays the Wisconsin transfer fee?
faqs.a: The seller does. The grantor is charged 30 cents per $100 of value, paid to the register of deeds when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: What does recording a deed cost?
faqs.a: A flat $30 per document. Copies of recorded papers cost $2 for the first page and $1 for each page after that, with $1 added if you want them certified.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee based on the sale price or the equity?
faqs.a: The sale price. For a sale, value includes everything paid or promised and any lien, so paying down your mortgage first does nothing to reduce the base the fee is figured on.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for the condition report?
faqs.a: Ten days after the offer is accepted. Miss it, and the buyer gets two business days to cancel and take back the deposit.

faqs.q: How long does my lender have to send a payoff statement?
faqs.a: Seven business days from your written request when the loan is secured by residential property. Expect the payoff amount and the daily interest on the statement.
